title: Student Loans
description: Federal and private, subsidized and not, and what the payment becomes.
wolfLine: The school ends. The loan does not. Know which kind you signed.

subsidized-loan.definition: A federal student loan where the government pays the interest while you are in school at least half time, and during the grace period.
subsidized-loan.example: A $3,500 subsidized loan sits through four years of school and adds $0 of interest while you are enrolled.

unsubsidized-loan.definition: A federal student loan where interest starts while you are still in school. You can pay it as you go, or let it be added to the balance.
unsubsidized-loan.example: $3,500 unsubsidized at 6% adds about $210 of interest in one year of school.

income-driven-repayment.definition: A federal plan that sets the monthly payment from your income and family size, instead of a fixed amount that clears the loan in 10 years.
income-driven-repayment.example: A standard plan might ask $180. An income-driven plan might ask $70 while your pay is low. The names and rules depend on when the loan was made.

lessons.title: Federal or Private
lessons.summary: Federal loans come with rules a bank loan does not have to offer.

steps.context: A federal student loan comes through the U.S. student-aid program. A private student loan comes from a bank or other lender. Federal loans can offer income-based payments and other protections. Private loans often start charging interest immediately and set their own rules.
steps.prompt: Which loan is made through the federal student-aid program?
choices: A private loan from a bank
steps.explain: Federal loans are the ones with the government rulebook.

steps.prompt: A private student loan has to offer the same repayment plans as a federal loan.
steps.explain: Private lenders set their own terms. Read them.

steps.prompt: You are offered both. Which one do people usually use first?
choices: The federal loan, and only then consider private
The private loan, because the ads are bigger
steps.explain: Federal loans first. Private loans fill a gap, they do not replace the safer option.

steps.prompt: Where do you check which federal plans your loan can use?
steps.explain: The official site. Plan names change, and 2026 is not 2019.

steps.prompt: Match the lender to the loan.
pairs: Not a student loan at all

steps.prompt: Putting tuition on a credit card is the same as a federal student loan.
steps.explain: A card has none of the federal protections, and a much higher rate.

lessons.title: Subsidized or Not
lessons.summary: One loan waits. The other starts the meter in the classroom.

steps.context: On a [[subsidized loan]], the government pays the interest while you are in school at least half time. On an [[unsubsidized loan]], interest starts right away. You can pay that interest while you study, or let it join the balance later.
steps.prompt: Who pays the interest on a subsidized loan while you are in school at least half time?
steps.explain: That is the subsidy.

steps.prompt: An unsubsidized loan charges no interest until you graduate.
steps.explain: The interest starts in school.

steps.prompt: Both loans are $3,500. Which one can grow while you are still in class?
steps.explain: Unsubsidized interest does not wait for graduation.

steps.prompt: You can pay the unsubsidized interest while you are in school. Why bother?
choices: So it is not added to the balance you repay later
steps.explain: Interest you let pile up becomes principal.

steps.prompt: The government covers in-school interest on a ___ loan.
steps.explain: Subsidized.

steps.prompt: Subsidized loans are limited. Not every student, and not every dollar, qualifies.
steps.explain: There are caps. Anything above them is often unsubsidized.

lessons.title: Amina’s Year in School
lessons.summary: Same dollar amount. Only one of the loans grows.

story.title: Two loans, one year
story.body:
Amina takes **$3,500** in a subsidized loan and **$3,500** in an unsubsidized loan for the year. The unsubsidized rate is **6%**.

She works part time and can spare **$20** a month. She wants to know what the unsubsidized loan costs if she lets the interest sit for this one year of school.

steps.prompt: Using simple interest, how much interest does the unsubsidized $3,500 add in one year at 6%?
steps.explain: $3,500 × 0.06 × 1 = $210. Real loans compound, so treat this as the clean estimate.

steps.prompt: How much interest does the subsidized $3,500 add during that same year in school?
steps.explain: $0. The government covers it while she is enrolled at least half time.

steps.prompt: If she pays $20 a month toward the unsubsidized interest, how much does she pay in a year?
Her $240 of payments against $210 of simple interest. What is true?
choices: She covered that year’s interest and a little more
She still owes all $210 on top
The subsidized loan also grew by $210
steps.explain: $240 − $210 = $30 to the good, on this simple estimate.

steps.prompt: Letting the $210 sit means she repays it later, with interest on a bigger balance.
steps.explain: Unpaid interest can be added to the principal.

steps.prompt: What is the careful habit for the unsubsidized loan?
choices: Pay the interest while she is in school, if the $20 fits
Ignore it until the bill is huge
Move it onto a credit card
steps.explain: Small payments now beat a larger balance later.

lessons.title: Before the First Bill
lessons.summary: Federal loans usually give you months after school, not a bill on graduation day.

steps.context: After you leave school, most federal loans wait about six months before the first bill. Interest on an unsubsidized loan still exists. A subsidized loan’s interest break usually covers this wait too. Confirm the date on studentaid.gov so it does not surprise you.
steps.prompt: Most federal student loans give you about how long after leaving school before payments start?
steps.explain: About six months. Use them. Do not spend them by accident.

steps.prompt: An unsubsidized loan stops charging interest during those six months.
steps.explain: The payment waits. The interest on an unsubsidized loan does not.

steps.prompt: Using half a year of 6% on the original $3,500, about how much interest builds in those 6 months?
What should you do during the six months?
choices: Find the servicer, set a payment method, and pick a plan before the first due date
Assume the loan ended with the classes
steps.explain: The pause is for getting ready, not for forgetting.

steps.prompt: You can apply for an income-driven plan before the first payment is due.
steps.explain: Doing it early means the first bill is the one you actually chose.

steps.prompt: Who tells you the real due date?
steps.explain: The servicer is the company that collects the payments.

lessons.title: Repayment Plans
lessons.summary: One plan is a fixed payoff. Another follows your paycheck. SAVE is not on the menu.

steps.title: What was true in 2026
steps.body:
A standard plan uses a fixed payment meant to clear the loan in about 10 years. An [[income-driven repayment]] plan sets the payment from your income instead.

The Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) plan ended in 2026 after a court order. Do not sign up for it. Which other plans you can use depends on when your loan was made. Check studentaid.gov before you pick.

steps.prompt: What does a standard plan try to do?
choices: Pay the loan off on a fixed schedule, often about 10 years
Set the payment from your income
steps.explain: Fixed payment, fixed clock.

steps.prompt: What does an income-driven plan look at?
steps.explain: The payment follows the paycheck. A lower payment can mean more interest over time.

steps.prompt: In 2026, new borrowers should enroll in the SAVE plan.
steps.explain: SAVE ended in 2026. Use the plans studentaid.gov still lists for your loan.

steps.prompt: A lower monthly payment under an income-driven plan can mean…
choices: You pay for longer, and you may pay more interest
steps.explain: Smaller is not the same as cheaper.

steps.prompt: Some balances can be forgiven after many years of qualifying payments. What is the careful take?
choices: Treat it as possible, and confirm the current rules on studentaid.gov before you count on a dollar
It is guaranteed for every loan
steps.explain: Programs exist. The details move. Education, not a promise.

lessons.title: The Loan Summary
lessons.summary: Principal, interest already added, and the payment they are asking.

steps.context: A loan summary shows what you borrowed, interest already added, and the payment of the plan you are on.

steps.prompt: The standard payment is $180 for 10 years (120 months). How much do you pay in total on that plan?
How much of that $21,600 is interest, above the $15,800 you owe today?
The $180 payment includes only the $15,800. Future interest is extra on top of the $21,600.
steps.explain: The $21,600 already includes the interest inside those 120 payments.

lessons.title: Choose the School with the Cost
lessons.summary: The job can be the same. The debt will not be.

steps.context: If two schools lead to the same work, the cheaper debt is the stronger start. Run the loans, not the brochure.
steps.prompt: How much more does School B cost in loans than School A?
The likely job is the same. Which leaving debt is easier to live with?
choices: They are equal because the job title matches
why: The title matches. The bill does not.
steps.explain: $22,000 less to repay.

steps.prompt: School A at a rough $200 a month would take how many months to pay $18,000, ignoring interest?
steps.explain: $18,000 ÷ $200 = 90 months, which is 7 years and 6 months. Interest makes it longer.

steps.prompt: A more expensive school is worth it whenever the campus is nicer.
steps.explain: Worth it depends on the pay you can earn and the debt you can carry.

steps.prompt: What belongs in the comparison?
choices: Loans at graduation, not just this year’s tuition sticker
steps.explain: The number you repay is the one that matters.

steps.prompt: You can work a year and cut School B’s loans by $8,000. What is the new gap versus School A’s $18,000?

lessons.title: Borrow Less Than They Offer
lessons.summary: The school can offer more than the degree is worth to you.

steps.context: An aid offer is a maximum, not a target. Every extra dollar is [[principal]] you repay with [[interest]].
steps.prompt: The aid letter offers $12,000. Your budget says you need $9,000. What can you do?
steps.explain: You can take less than the offer.

steps.prompt: You decline $3,000 of the offer. At 5% simple interest for 4 years in school, about how much unsubsidized interest do you avoid?
steps.explain: $3,000 × 0.05 × 4 = $600, before any interest after graduation.

steps.prompt: Taking the maximum loan is required if you want the classes.
steps.explain: Borrow what you need. Leave the rest.

steps.prompt: Those $3,000, repaid later as $75 a month, take how many months if you ignore interest?
What is a practical way to need less?
choices: A cheaper term, a scholarship, or working a few shifts
steps.explain: Fewer dollars borrowed is the only guaranteed forgiveness.

steps.prompt: An aid offer is a ___, not a bill you must borrow in full.
steps.explain: You can borrow less.
